A San Francisco startup founder claims he’s been forced to relocate his office after dog attacks — including one that sent his friend to the hospital with a “really bad” leg wound.

Anto Patrex, founder of AI robotics startup Cosmic Brain, says he’s relocated his firm from a tech incubator space on Market Street to the safer Dogpatch neighborhood after he and a friend were  attacked by dogs within the span of a few days.

“Two weeks ago I was walking down Sixth Street, and there was a bulldog I didn’t see that came out of a wheelchair — it rushed at me and bit my leg,” Patrex said.

“The week after, my friend was walking through the same street and was bit … it was a very bad wound, he was rushed to the hospital,” he added.

“There have been a lot of dog cases in the area.”

Patrex elaborated in an X post, saying the frightening dog encounters along with “shattered car glass on every block” and other crimes had led him to move his office after 12 months.

He attached videos from local X creator JJ Smith depicting blight in the area surrounding his office location.

The techie described an incident in which several engineer friends were waiting in line for ice cream when a crazed man managed to rip down a road sign, attempting to strike bystanders with it.

“They ran — everyone carries pepper spray,” Patrex said.

City data shows dozens of dog attacks in San Francisco’s Tenderloin neighborhood, with 74 attacks reported between January and September, KRON4 reported.

officially moving our office out of downtown SF after 12 months on Market Street.a space that incubated over 100 startups just a few years ago is down to fewer than 10 teams today. the physical reality of working here took a heavy toll. getting chased down the sidewalk by an… pic.twitter.com/lei1VLEdsj

In September, a woman was mauled by a pitbull and left with life-threatening injuries in a horrifying incident caught on video. In the disturbing footage, bystanders screamed and desperately tried to pull the beast away before police officers finally secured the dog.

The animal collapsed and died at the scene.

San Francisco’s Sixth Street corridor, located near downtown and the Tenderloin neighborhood, is a notorious hotspot for drug dealing and petty crime.

Market Street, San Francisco’s main thoroughfare that was once a world-class retail destination, has struggled with drugs and street crime, particularly at night.

The main drag was once home to Twitter, Uber and Block, but tech companies have fled the area or gone remote, leaving the area littered with vacancies. The mid-Market area had a 32% vacancy rate  in the third quarter of this year, according to Kidder Matthews.

Patrex said he’d prefer to work downtown in order to more easily meet investors and partners, but he and his colleagues needed to be “safe.” “That sucks too,” he said.

Anto Patrex, founder of AI robotics startup Cosmic Brain, says he’s relocated his firm from a tech incubator space on Market Street to the safer Dogpatch neighborhood after he and a friend were  attacked by dogs within the span of a few days.

“Two weeks ago I was walking down Sixth Street, and there was a bulldog I didn’t see that came out of a wheelchair — it rushed at me and bit my leg,” Patrex said.

“The week after, my friend was walking through the same street and was bit … it was a very bad wound, he was rushed to the hospital,” he added.

“There have been a lot of dog cases in the area.”

Patrex elaborated in an X post, saying the frightening dog encounters along with “shattered car glass on every block” and other crimes had led him to move his office after 12 months.

He attached videos from local X creator JJ Smith depicting blight in the area surrounding his office location.

The techie described an incident in which several engineer friends were waiting in line for ice cream when a crazed man managed to rip down a road sign, attempting to strike bystanders with it.

“They ran — everyone carries pepper spray,” Patrex said.

City data shows dozens of dog attacks in San Francisco’s Tenderloin neighborhood, with 74 attacks reported between January and September, KRON4 reported.

In September, a woman was mauled by a pitbull and left with life-threatening injuries in a horrifying incident caught on video. In the disturbing footage, bystanders screamed and desperately tried to pull the beast away before police officers finally secured the dog.

The animal collapsed and died at the scene.

San Francisco’s Sixth Street corridor, located near downtown and the Tenderloin neighborhood, is a notorious hotspot for drug dealing and petty crime.

Market Street, San Francisco’s main thoroughfare that was once a world-class retail destination, has struggled with drugs and street crime, particularly at night.

The main drag was once home to Twitter, Uber and Block, but tech companies have fled the area or gone remote, leaving the area littered with vacancies. The mid-Market area had a 32% vacancy rate  in the third quarter of this year, according to Kidder Matthews.

Patrex said he’d prefer to work downtown in order to more easily meet investors and partners, but he and his colleagues needed to be “safe.” “That sucks too,” he said.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Pete DeBoer saw it first with Joe Thornton when he was in San Jose, then with Joe Pavelski while in Dallas. Now, it is 35-year-old Brayden Schenn on Long Island playing the role, “on the back nine” of his career, of a leading voice and mentor in the dressing room, while maintaining a high level of play in his own right.

“He recognizes he was brought in here as much for his intangibles as what he brings on the ice,” DeBoer said Thursday before the Islanders faced Carolina. “I think he understands that. I think he’s taken that piece of it and really embraced it.”

Indeed, as much as Schenn struggled last season upon arriving as the Islanders’ big-ticket acquisition at the trade deadline, one wonders if general manager Mathieu Darche is itching to find the nearest microphone and declare, “I told you so.”

Schenn not only has stepped seamlessly into a leadership role in the Islanders dressing room, he is centering a trio with Emil Heineman and Victor Eklund that’s been the club’s most consistent line of late.

The difference between walking in midseason when cracks were already starting to form in the Islanders foundation and getting to participate in building the foundation from training camp onwards has been massive. Schenn has four goals and five assists through 14 games, has fit like a glove in DeBoer’s system and when asked about all of this Thursday morning, sheepishly replied, “I hate talking about myself.”

That is, of course, exactly how the Islanders want their older, example-setting veterans to respond to such a question. Schenn did acquiesce to explaining the added comfort he has with the Islanders now, as opposed to when he arrived in March.

“I would say it’s just everything. It’s not one thing,” he said. “You can’t pinpoint one thing and say that’s why. I think it’s, one, coming here, gotta prove yourself every single day in this league. You get a great opportunity to play with great linemates. The organization and the guys in the locker room have been awesome to us since Day 1 we’ve been here. So as you get more comfortable around the room, being around people, it just allows you to be yourself a little more. I still feel like I got better.”

Knowing his teammates and having training camp to develop chemistry makes a huge difference, as has DeBoer’s presence behind the bench.

“I really enjoy playing for Pete. He’s a smart coach,” Schenn said. “I’ve learned a lot from him. Very good systematically, defensively. With a coach like that, as long as you’re bringing your effort within the system each night, he’s gonna reward the guys who want to do that. I think as a group, as a whole, we have a bunch of guys with complete buy-in who’ve realistically given ourselves a chance in every game.”

DeBoer took notice on a recent off day when he and the injured players were the only people at the facility. When DeBoer left, Schenn pulled in with his car.

“I’m sure he got his kids off to school and headed to the rink after that,” DeBoer said. “You can tell the guys who just love the process of it. He’s one of those guys.”

Indeed, DeBoer added that Schenn has the qualities of a future head coach. Heineman, his linemate, sounded similar notes.

“He [had been] been a captain [in St. Louis] for a long time. It shows on how he acts as a human being in the locker room and on the ice,” Heineman told The Post. “… You can tell right away he has a lot of experience in the league. He’s won [a Stanley Cup]. He knows what it takes.”

news.originalContent:
Parliament’s approval lays the groundwork for further Turkish involvement in Saudi Arabia’s conflict with the Houthis.

Turkiye’s parliament has ratified a defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan that includes a collective defence clause, committing NATO’s second-largest military to the group’s aid in case of attack.

The ratification on Thursday comes as Riyadh continues to face attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis.

Turkiye first signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August and sent it to parliament for ratification last month.

Article 1 of a bill approving the pact was adopted by the Turkish parliament on Wednesday.

But afterwards, Deputy Parliament Speaker Celal Adan adjourned the session until Thursday afternoon, the Anadolu news agency reported.

After parliament returned to session, lawmakers continued to debate the other articles in the pact.

The agreement ultimately passed with 279 votes in favour and 119 against, with 398 of the chamber’s 592 lawmakers taking part in the vote.

The pact contains 16 articles, according to a document submitted to the Turkish parliament, seen by the Reuters news agency.

In Article 1 of the accord, the signatories shall use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity. Article 1 can be invoked in case of an attack on any member state.

Once the first article is invoked, the document lays out provisions for what follows.

“In the event one of the parties is subjected to an armed attack or military aggression by another country or group of countries, the parties shall immediately provide assistance to the party under attack, utilising the full range of mutual assistance measures available to them,” says Article 2 of the pact.

This key clause mirrors Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, the document that established the NATO military alliance. NATO’s Article 5 establishes that an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

Given that Turkiye is a member of both NATO and the Mecca pact, critics have raised questions about whether the country’s government might face a conflict of interest in allocating its military resources.

Turkish officials, however, have dismissed such concerns as unfounded.

Other articles in the Mecca pact concern a mutual agreement to increase defence industry cooperation and military coordination, with the aim of deterring threats.

Those articles, in part, commit member states to conducting joint training, pursuing technological innovation and sharing logistics and intelligence resources.

The draft approved by Turkish lawmakers commits member countries to the pact for 10 years, after which point they may withdraw.

It also leaves open the possibility of other countries joining, with the approval of the pact’s existing members. Syria’s government has already expressed interest.

Despite Thursday’s parliamentary ratification, it is not a foregone conclusion that Turkish troops would be deployed to Saudi Arabia amid the Houthi attacks.

Experts say any Turkish troop deployment would also require other legislative processes.

Turkiye’s Defence Minister Yasar Guler said in October that the scope of potential support for Saudi Arabia would be determined after ratification.

“We absolutely do not foresee entering into any conflict with the Houthis,” Turkish media reported Guler as saying. Instead, Turkish support “would be to strengthen deterrence”.

Tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen had abated somewhat following a 2022 ceasefire. But the Houthis have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent months, notably launching a series of deadly strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

The region also remains embroiled in the US-Israel war on Iran, which has contributed to cross-border tensions.

On Thursday, Saudi Arabia announced it had intercepted a drone in the region of Medina. Riyadh has accused the Houthis several times of targeting Mecca and Medina, two holy cities in Islam, an accusation the Iran-backed group systematically rejects.

news.originalContent:
Trump again said a major Russia-Ukraine deal is ‘very close’, but gave no specifics.

US President Donald Trump has said that a deal between Russia and Ukraine may be imminent, following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, at the White House.

“I think we’re going to be very close to settling Russia-Ukraine,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday, while declining to disclose details of his conversation with Dmitriev.

“There’s going to be an agreement. It’s going to be a big agreement, and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” Trump said, adding that the effort could include “all of Europe”.

Trump has frequently predicted that an agreement to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II was close. Negotiations have, however, picked up in recent weeks.

Trump said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation on Thursday.

The meeting between the US president and Dmitriev came after a diplomatic gathering hosted by First Lady Melania Trump, which brought Russian and Ukrainian representatives together to mark and build on the localised six-day truce she helped broker in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky in October. The US president did not attend the event.

The temporary ceasefire ran from October 27 to November 1 and allowed for the evacuation of nearly 800 civilians from the besieged, Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, as well as the delivery of critical food and medical supplies.

Senior officials from both countries attended on Thursday, including Dmitriev; Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner; David Arakhamia, leader of the Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament; and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary human rights commissioner.

Melania Trump also spoke at the event, which the White House described as “the first time in American history that a First Lady has personally brought representatives of two nations at war to the White House for diplomacy”.

“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,” she said, urging both sides to see the humanitarian truce in Oleshky “as a spark in a world of darkness”.

The first lady presented Putin’s and Zelenskyy’s representatives with large white envelopes and asked them to deliver her personal letters to each leader. Dmitriev presented her with a painting by an 11-year-old girl, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sent her the Order of Princess Olga, a Ukrainian award recognising her role in the ceasefire.

news.originalContent:
DSA-backed Raman will lead America’s second largest city, promising action on homelessness and affordable housing.

Nithya Raman, a progressive Los Angeles City Council member, has defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, putting her on track to become the first South Asian to lead the second-largest city in the United States.

The Associated Press called the race for Raman on Thursday, with Raman holding 52 percent of the vote.

Raman, 45, overtook Bass despite the incumbent’s support from prominent Democrats such as California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.

Her campaign was backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), with her victory coming as part of a surge in visibility and electoral wins for the left-wing political movement.

A record number of candidates backed or affiliated with the DSA won federal offices in Tuesday’s midterm elections. On its website, the DSA has claimed credit for contributing to at least 300 candidacies or ballot referendums during the midterms, and it said it is on track to count 105 of those as victories.

Some of those wins came in congressional races, with figures such as Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez, Melat Kiros and Chris Rabb winning their first terms as US representatives.

Raman’s victory in Los Angeles follows another high-profile democratic socialist winning a mayor’s race in New York City last year: Zohran Mamdani.

Raman was born in India and worked as an urban planner before running for office. Once an ally of Bass, she had initially endorsed her re-election campaign but reversed course, entering the mayoral race in February, just hours before the filing deadline.

In her victory speech, Raman promised to restore what she called an ambitious, creative and entrepreneurial Los Angeles.

“For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do,” she told the crowd.

Raman also pledged to expand affordable housing, improve neglected city services and take a different approach to homelessness by deploying more medical teams to assist people who are unhoused.

In addition, she called for replacing the city’s police chief over concerns about cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Raman now faces the task of delivering on those promises in a city of more than 3.8 million people.

Los Angeles also faces the challenge of hosting the 2028 Olympic Games, which open in July of that year.

With the result, Bass has become the first Los Angeles mayor in more than two decades to lose a re-election bid.

news.originalContent:
Melat Kiros becomes the first Generation Z woman elected to Congress, embodying a new era of political representation.

The outcome of the 2026 US midterm elections has marked a historic shift in American politics, with diverse candidates winning office and the first Generation Z woman elected to Congress.

Of the 117 Generation Z candidates who ran for Congress this year, 24 won their primaries and made it to Tuesday’s ballot, according to the organisation Future Caucus.

Among them was Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old Ethiopian-born democratic socialist from Colorado, who became the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress.

Kiros, a lawyer turned doctoral student, won a stunning primary victory earlier this year, with the first-time candidate beating 30-year incumbent Representative Diana DeGette in the Denver-area seat.

After winning the primary, she told supporters that she was taking the fight to “Donald Trump and the oligarchy”, abolishing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), passing Medicare for All and ending the “genocide in Palestine”.

She joins Representative Maxwell Frost of Florida, who became the first Gen Z member of the House in 2022.

Young people voted overwhelmingly for Democrats, according to an Associated Press news agency voter poll.

After relatively high support for Trump in the 2024 election, young voters snapped back towards the Democratic Party in this year’s midterms.

The AP Voter Poll showed about seven in 10 voters under 30 nationally said they supported the Democratic candidate in their local US House race, while about three in 10 said they voted for the Republican. That was a dramatic shift from 2024, when the youngest voters were roughly split between Trump and Kamala Harris.

Most first-time midterm voters, who skew younger, also supported the Democratic candidate.

Both young voters and first-time voters made up a fairly small share of the electorate. Only about one in 10 voters in the 2026 national electorate are under 30, for instance, which limited the impact of the shift.

But young voters’ displeasure with the country and its leadership was clear. About half of young voters said they were “angry” about the way things were going in the country, compared with only about one-third of voters aged 65 and older. And about six in 10 voters under 30 said one reason for their vote for the US House was to express opposition to Trump, compared with about half of voters aged 30-44 and about four in 10 voters aged 45 and older.

Young voters shifted towards the Democrats in each of the Senate races where the Democratic Party picked up a seat, including in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina.

news.originalContent:
The ANC was on about 32 percent of the vote after almost half of the votes were counted in municipal elections.

South Africa’s early municipal election results have shown the African National Congress (ANC) with a sharply reduced vote share, weakening the long-dominant party’s control of key cities such as Johannesburg.

The ANC was on about 32 percent of the vote, with the Democratic Alliance (DA) in second place at 25 percent, after more than 60 percent of the votes had been counted in this week’s municipal elections, data from the election commission showed late on Thursday.

Meanwhile, former President Jacob Zuma’s breakaway opposition uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party was in third place with 8.5 percent, below levels suggested by opinion polls.

About 15.9 million of 29.2 million registered voters cast ballots, the electoral commission said, putting turnout at an estimated 54.5 percent, up from 46 percent in the pandemic-hit 2021 local elections.

The ANC, which has been South Africa’s largest party since it led the country out of apartheid in 1994, has tended to do worse in municipal elections than nationally and has acknowledged its failures in local governance.

From nearly 70 percent of the national vote in 2004, the ANC fell below 50 percent for the first time in the 2021 municipal elections, winning 46 percent.

At the 2024 national elections, it managed just more than 40 percent and was forced to accept a unity government with nine other parties, including the DA.

The party, now led by President Cyril Ramaphosa, has borne the brunt of criticism about years of municipal mismanagement that have left South Africans grappling with failing water supplies, persistent power cuts and crumbling public services.

It has also faced corruption allegations, while splinter parties have eaten away at its support base.

The results of this week’s local ballot will offer a key measure of voters’ sentiment ahead of the 2029 general election.

Control of the country’s eight major metropolitan municipalities is up for grabs, alongside dozens of district and local councils.

The MK party had been tipped as one of the few parties capable of securing an outright majority in the eastern port city of Durban.

But projections by the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a state-funded research body, put its support there at 32 percent.

The DA, meanwhile, was forecast to retain control of tourist magnet Cape Town with 56 percent of the vote, with its leader, Geordin Hill-Lewis, already declaring victory.

The party was also leading with 34 percent in Johannesburg, the country’s financial capital, after running a spirited campaign spearheaded by its former leader, Helen Zille, 75, according to CSIR projections.

With outright majorities far from assured in several major cities, the results could usher in another round of complex coalition negotiations, with parties bargaining to assemble the alliances needed to govern.

Final results are expected on Sunday.

news.originalContent:
Former Trump lawyer Alina Habba laughed off a question from CBS News about whether she would consider donating fees she made in a reported $50 million pardon deal to President Trump’s library.

Habba reportedly signed a four-year, $50 million agreement to become general counsel for Concord Partners, a company established in October 2025 by the daughter of Venezuelan-Italian banker Julio Herrera Velutini, while serving as a U.S. attorney and senior adviser in New Jersey and the Department of Justice. She officially began the role at Concord on Jan. 1, and Herrera Velutini, who was charged by the Biden DOJ for his role in a Puerto Rican bribery scheme, later received a full presidential pardon from Trump on Jan. 15. (RELATED: Pete Hegseth’s Wife Gets In On Trump 2.0’s Lucrative Swamp Bonanza)

For a report on Trump’s presidential library, CBS News asked Habba whether she would consider donating the pardon deal fees to the library or another Trump-related entity. Habba responded “haha” before quickly deleting the text and declining to comment, according to CBS News.

Former Trump lawyer Alina Habba - asked by @CBSNews if she will donate her fees from a contract tied to the family of a businessman Mr. Trump pardoned - responded to the text with a “haha” reaction then removed it Comes after @tylerpager reporting in NYT on Trump telling aides/allies she should donate

Trump publicly rebuked Habba in late October, telling reporters at a Mar-a-Lago Halloween party that Habba entering into the deal was “totally obnoxious and outrageous.”

“I thought it was terrible,” he said. “I told her, and I said, ‘I don’t want her paid.’ I thought we had somebody speak to the people that did it, and she used her relationship to do that. And it was far too much.”

The president also criticized Habba privately among aides and allies when he learned of the deal, first reported by The New York Times, and said that she should donate a portion of the money to his future presidential library. Trump, however, said on Halloween that he was not expecting Habba to do it but suggested someone from Herrera Velutini’s family should.

“I expect maybe the people,” he said of the family. “I don’t know if anybody wants to make it. But it’s unacceptable what she did.”

news.originalContent:
College Republicans’ populist faction made a stunning break with President Donald Trump over Tuesday’s blue tsunami and the administration’s broken promises.

The College Republican Patriot Coalition (CRPC), a consortium of college Republican groups across the country that align with America First, “unequivocally” laid the blame for the GOP’s historic losses “at the feet of the Trump administration and the Republican Party.” (RELATED: ‘No Downside’: Iran War Hawks Get A Midterm Reality Check)

“This outcome was no accident,” the group said in a statement. “It is the predictable result of an administration and a party that campaigned on America First and governed as though we would wait forever. This lame duck Republican government failed to do what it promised, and manipulated and insulted its base for sounding the alarms for two years.”

America First is the ONLY way forward. Official CRPC statement on the results of last night’s midterm election: https://t.co/GKOuzCAXNe

“Millions of us young Americans knocked on doors, made calls, and cast first-time ballots for a movement that promised affordability, mass deportations, reindustrialization, and an end to foreign wars,” CRPC continued. “Instead, we received a war on behalf of Israel, stunted deportations, and a flailing economy. On all fronts, the Republican Party and the Trump administration in particular has betrayed us.”

CRPC urged Trump to “purge his administration of those who have not and will not deliver on the mandate voters gave him in 2024,” immediately end the Iran War and focus instead on the affordability crisis that has led to young Americans “being priced out of their own country.” (RELATED: Ron DeSantis Says 2026 Midterms ‘Close To An Extinction-Level Event’ For GOP)

The group also singled out the “disastrous and unintelligible” Iran War as the administration’s “greatest betrayal.”

“President Trump promised ‘no new wars,’ and millions of us believed him,” CRPC said. “This administration broke that promise and dragged us into another endless conflict with Iran at the urging of Israel.”

“Yesterday’s defeat was not inflicted by the left and is not the fault of the Republican base, but lies squarely at the feet of this administration’s broken promises,” the group concluded. “Americans deserve more than broken promises. We deserve a true champion that will put America first.”

یک هواپیمای ایرباس متعلق به شرکت «ایر لینگوس» ایرلند که صبح پنجشنبه از دوبلین برخاسته بود، با اعلام وضعیت اضطراری، تغییر مسیر داد و در پایگاه هوایی «اورو» در شمال فرانسه فرود آمد.

شرکت هواپیمایی «فین‌ایر» فنلاند هم اعلام کرد که روز پنجشنبه یکی از هواپیماهایش که از هلسینکی به پایتخت ایتالیا در حال پرواز بود، تهدید به بمب‌گذاری شد.

این هواپیما توسط جت‌های نیروی هوایی اسکورت شد و طبق برنامه فرود آمد.

گزارش‌های دیگری هم از تهدید به بمب‌گذاری هواپیماهای اروپایی در روز پنجشنبه منتشر شده است.

در پراگ پلیس جمهوری چک اعلام کرد که در پی دریافت تهدیدهایی درباره وجود یک «بمب دست‌ساز»، چهار هواپیما را بازرسی کرده اما ماده منفجره‌ای پیدا نکرده است.

این اتفاق دو روز پس از آن است که حداقل هفت پرواز اروپایی، از جمله دو پرواز از مبدا بریتانیا، هدف تهدیدهای مشکوک به بمب‌گذاری قرار گرفتند.

البته پس از جستجو، هیچ ماده منفجره‌ای در هواپیماها یافت نشد.

گزیده‌ای از مهم‌ترین خبرها، گزارش‌های میدانی و گفت‌وگوهای اختصاصی را هر هفته در ایمیل خود دریافت کنید.

بیانیه‌ شرکت هواپیمایی «ایر لینگوس» تایید کرده است که پرواز دوبلین-رم، «صبح امروز به عنوان یک اقدام احتیاطی امنیتی، به سمت نرماندی تغییر مسیر داد.»

در ادامه این بیانیه آمده است که «این پرواز به‌سلامت به زمین نشست و ایرلینگوس تلاش خواهد کرد تا در اسرع وقت، تمهیدات لازم برای انتقال مسافران به مقصد نهایی‌شان را فراهم کند.»

در همین حال، یک پرواز شرکت هواپیمایی «ویز ایر» که از میلان عازم ورشو بود هم پیش از تغییر مسیر به سمت وین، پایتخت اتریش، وضعیت اضطراری اعلام کرد.

هرچند گزارشی مبنی بر تهدید بمب‌گذاری وجود نداشت و علت آن نامشخص است.

در روز پنجشنبه چندین هواپیما پس از دریافت تهدید به بمب‌گذاری، بازرسی شدند.

دو مورد از این هواپیماها مربوط به بریتانیا بود؛ یک پرواز از مبدا منچستر که در منطقه خودمختار مورسیا در اسپانیا به زمین نشست، و دیگری پروازی از فرودگاه هیتروی لندن به مقصد ورشو در لهستان.

منابعی در فرودگاه «فیومیچینو» در رم به بی‌بی‌سی گفتند که دو پرواز شرکت «رایان‌ایر»، یکی از مبدا دوبلین و دیگری از لیسبون پرتغال، پس از فرود در رم و در پی دریافت هشدارهایی ناشناس مورد بازرسی قرار گرفتند، اما هیچ‌گونه مواد منفجره‌ای پیدا نشد.

این منابع افزودند که کارشناسان خنثی‌سازی بمب پلیس، پروتکل‌های امنیتی استاندارد را برای تضمین امنیت تمامی مسافران و خدمه اجرا کردند و پس از آن، وضعیت هشدار پایان یافت.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump is signaling immigration cooperation with Democrats as Vice President JD Vance warns against amnesty.

During an interview Tuesday on Fox News’ election night coverage, President Trump spoke with hosts Martha MacCallum and Bret Baier about whether he expects Democrats to work with him when the new Congress takes office in January. (RELATED: Trump Says He Can Work With Dems On Immigration After GOP Gets Smoked In Midterms)

Baier asked whether Democrats, despite what Trump has called “Trump Derangement Syndrome,” would be willing to work with him and send legislation to his desk that he could sign.

🚨 JUST NOW: President Trump reveals he’s looking to do possible IMMIGRATION DEALS with Democrats, but they AREN’T in control because HE has the veto pen "They can send over 50 different great bills that they’re all excited about and I send them back with a nice stamp veto and, you know, there’s not a thing they can do about that." "I’m a person that likes getting things done…immigration is a big deal. I’ve always felt we should be able to work at immigration." That is, if it’s NO AMNESTY 🇺🇸🇺🇸 The American people do NOT want amnesty.

Trump acknowledged that Democrats would be “in control but not in control,” noting he retains veto power and hopes he will not have to use it.

“I’m a person that likes getting things done, and there are things that we can work with. We can’t work on everything.”

Trump specifically pointed to immigration as an area where he believes the two parties could find common ground.

“But I can work with them on a lot of things. I mean, we can work with them on immigration. I think. Immigration is a big deal. I’ve always felt we should be able to work on immigration.”

Still, in comments exclusive to the Daily Caller, a White House official emphasized that mass amnesty for illegal immigrants is not on the table.

Trump’s comments come as Democrats across the country have criticized his administration’s immigration enforcement efforts, with some campaigning on promises to abolish ICE or restrict its operations. (RELATED: GOP Lawmaker Mike Lawler Attempts To Resurrect Amnesty Plan)

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) approved two resolutions in August calling for changes to immigration enforcement, including one urging Congress to abolish ICE and phase out the immigration detention system, according to a Newsweek report.

The resolutions also called for restricting Department of Homeland Security funding unless the agency ends certain enforcement operations, including workplace raids, mass arrests and immigration actions near schools and places of worship.

They also called for ending contracts with private immigration detention companies.

The developments come as Republicans grapple with losses in both chambers of Congress.

Vance offered his first assessment of the midterm results in a post on X, arguing that voter frustration over the war, rather than poor turnout, drove many 2024 Trump voters to defect to Democrats.

He said Republicans must refocus on ending the war, lowering living costs, advancing America First policies, and reassessing the U.S. relationship with Israel to win back voters who abandoned the party.

Vance also warned Republicans against embracing amnesty as a solution to the party’s political struggles, accusing establishment politicians of “gaslighting” voters.

“In the next few months, there’s going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you,” Vance wrote.

One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we’re going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us." Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026. There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were: 1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.) In the next few months, there’s going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there. I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

The Caller asked the White House if amnesty would be on the table following Trump’s indication that he would be willing to work with Democrats on immigration.

A White House official wrote, “There has never been a stronger administration on immigration enforcement than the Trump Administration. Both the President and Vice President have delivered the most secure border in American history and under their leadership, ICE has shattered arrest records. The Administration will never allow for mass amnesty.”

Trump has consistently taken a hard-line stance on immigration, making the issue a central focus of his political career and a defining priority of his administration. Immigration played a major role in his 2016, 2020, and 2024 presidential campaigns, and his administration has pursued an aggressive deportation agenda since returning to office.

Despite some rumblings that the administration could be more flexible on the subject after the midterm losses, a source familiar with internal discussions told the Daily Caller that “amnesty is not on the table” when asked whether the administration was considering changes to its immigration policy.

Trump was also asked about Vance’s assessment of the midterm results Wednesday during an event at the White House ballroom construction site, saying the vice president’s post “was fine. I thought it was good.” (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: More Foreign Nationals Come Under ICE Scrutiny For Alleged Illegal Voting)

He also acknowledged that the conflict had driven up gas prices in the short term but defended the decision to launch military action.

“I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term, and probably that’s probably true. But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again, because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear war.”

President Donald J. Trump on Vice President JD Vance’s statement: “I thought it was good.” https://t.co/g1fJ4wk70W

Trump did not address Vance’s separate comments on immigration or his warning against amnesty.

Meanwhile, NBC News exit polls found that voters preferred Republicans over Democrats on handling immigration, with 44 percent saying the GOP was better equipped to handle the issue, compared to roughly 40 percent to 41 percent who favored Democrats.

Several Republicans who backed the Dignity Act, a sweeping immigration proposal that supporters have pitched as a way to curb illegal immigration, overhaul the asylum system and provide legal status for long-term undocumented immigrants, also lost their House seats. (RELATED: GOP Lawmaker Mike Lawler Attempts To Resurrect Amnesty Plan)

Those lawmakers include Republican Reps. David Valadao of California, Monica De La Cruz of Texas, Mike Lawler of New York, Gabe Evans of Colorado and Jen Kiggans of Virginia.

Valadao, Lawler and Evans were original co-sponsors of the legislation, while De La Cruz and Kiggans later signed on as co-sponsors.

The bill’s sponsor, Republican Florida Rep. Maria Salazar, retained her seat.

Immigration was the only issue on which Republicans held an advantage, while Democrats led on several other issues, including the economy in some polling breakdowns.

The Caller reached out to the White House for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.

There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we’re going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us." Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026. There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were: 1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.) In the next few months, there’s going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there. I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

The Caller asked the White House if amnesty would be on the table following Trump’s indication that he would be willing to work with Democrats on immigration.

A White House official wrote, “There has never been a stronger administration on immigration enforcement than the Trump Administration. Both the President and Vice President have delivered the most secure border in American history and under their leadership, ICE has shattered arrest records. The Administration will never allow for mass amnesty.”

Trump has consistently taken a hard-line stance on immigration, making the issue a central focus of his political career and a defining priority of his administration. Immigration played a major role in his 2016, 2020, and 2024 presidential campaigns, and his administration has pursued an aggressive deportation agenda since returning to office.

Despite some rumblings that the administration could be more flexible on the subject after the midterm losses, a source familiar with internal discussions told the Daily Caller that “amnesty is not on the table” when asked whether the administration was considering changes to its immigration policy.

Trump was also asked about Vance’s assessment of the midterm results Wednesday during an event at the White House ballroom construction site, saying the vice president’s post “was fine. I thought it was good.” (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: More Foreign Nationals Come Under ICE Scrutiny For Alleged Illegal Voting)

He also acknowledged that the conflict had driven up gas prices in the short term but defended the decision to launch military action.

“I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term, and probably that’s probably true. But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again, because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear war.”

President Donald J. Trump on Vice President JD Vance’s statement: “I thought it was good.” https://t.co/g1fJ4wk70W

Trump did not address Vance’s separate comments on immigration or his warning against amnesty.

Meanwhile, NBC News exit polls found that voters preferred Republicans over Democrats on handling immigration, with 44 percent saying the GOP was better equipped to handle the issue, compared to roughly 40 percent to 41 percent who favored Democrats.

Several Republicans who backed the Dignity Act, a sweeping immigration proposal that supporters have pitched as a way to curb illegal immigration, overhaul the asylum system and provide legal status for long-term undocumented immigrants, also lost their House seats. (RELATED: GOP Lawmaker Mike Lawler Attempts To Resurrect Amnesty Plan)

Those lawmakers include Republican Reps. David Valadao of California, Monica De La Cruz of Texas, Mike Lawler of New York, Gabe Evans of Colorado and Jen Kiggans of Virginia.

Valadao, Lawler and Evans were original co-sponsors of the legislation, while De La Cruz and Kiggans later signed on as co-sponsors.

The bill’s sponsor, Republican Florida Rep. Maria Salazar, retained her seat.

Immigration was the only issue on which Republicans held an advantage, while Democrats led on several other issues, including the economy in some polling breakdowns.

The Caller reached out to the White House for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.

Illustration by Daily Caller Staff; with Getty Images

Hey y’all, welcome back to Unfit to Print.

We’re doing something a little bit different today.

CONSERVATISM AT A CROSSROADS

Republicans just lost both chambers of Congress, and the party has some serious soul-searching to do.

President Donald Trump has been the center of Republican politics for more than a decade.

He shattered the old GOP consensus on immigration, trade, foreign policy, and the relationship between the party and working-class Americans.

But identifying the failures of the party is not the same thing as building a durable political movement to replace it.

There’s an important distinction between MAGA and America First. MAGA is a movement built around Trump. America First is a governing philosophy that predates him and ought to outlast him. Trump may have brought those principles back into the political mainstream, but he doesn’t have a monopoly on defining them.

The conservative movement now faces an important question: What does America First actually mean beyond Trump? And who gets to set the agenda?

You may think these questions are premature. Trump is staring down a lame-duck presidency, but he still has at least two years as the de facto leader of the party. He’ll also have a major say in who inherits his political mantle in 2028.

My former boss Geoffrey Ingersoll, however, once said something really important about political media and the Daily Caller’s role in it: “It’s like pursuing a football on the football field. You want to go to where it’s going. You don’t want to go to where it is.”

That philosophy has stuck with me, and it’s a big part of how I think about my job as editor-in-chief.

The Daily Caller’s responsibility isn’t just to cover whoever is feuding on the Hill, what bill is being introduced in Congress, where the president’s next rally is going to be, or even who won the midterms.

Our job is to identify and cover the issues, ideas, and tensions that are going to shape American politics — and your lives — in the future, without waiting for permission from Washington’s political establishment.

That approach has ruffled some feathers.

Semafor published a piece Sunday about the Daily Caller’s editorial direction under my leadership, titled “More MAGA than MAGA: How the Daily Caller turned on MAGA and Trump.”

The article focused heavily on our coverage of the war with Iran, Israeli influence in Washington, and the backlash we’ve received for daring to question uniparty orthodoxy.

I spoke to the author of the article for about 45 minutes. He included just one of my quotes: “The Iran war is a huge turning point for the conservative movement.”

But the reporter didn’t include anything I said after that.

What I explained is that the war is exposing tensions within the MAGA coalition that have existed since Trump first brought it together.

Trump’s coalition shared a distrust of Washington, resentment toward the political class, and a desire to put American interests first. But beneath that broad agreement were competing ideas about the role of government, the economy, foreign policy, and the relationship between ordinary Americans and powerful institutions.

For years, Trump’s personality helped paper over those differences.

Now, those disagreements are coming to a head.

For years, Trump railed against forever wars and promised to put American interests first. Now the United States is stuck in another quagmire in the Middle East, and conservatives are confronting fundamental disagreements about what the America First approach is to military intervention, foreign alliances, our obligations to other countries, and the impact on Americans’ pocketbooks.

Meanwhile, young Americans are struggling to find jobs, afford homes, get married, and start families. American workers are confronting the consequences of legal and illegal immigration, artificial intelligence and automation, and an economy that’s increasingly dominated by powerful corporations. The proliferation of online pornography and gambling is raising serious questions about addiction, socialization, and community. Americans also remain suspicious of government surveillance, censorship, and the influence of wealthy donors and special interests.

And we’re taking a particularly hard look at foreign influence in Washington, whether it’s coming from Israel, China, or any other country seeking to shape American policy. The question isn’t whether we consider a particular nation a friend or an adversary. It’s whether its interests are being placed ahead of those of the American people.

These are precisely the issues we’ve been putting front and center at the Daily Caller.

Frankly, I don’t think the question should be why we’re covering these issues. It should be why more conservative media outlets aren’t.

Semafor describes us as “more MAGA than MAGA,” but that misses the point. We’re not competing for the title of Trump’s most faithful disciples. We’re asking hard questions about whether the movement that promised to shake up Washington is actually changing it — or simply replacing one set of powerful interests with another.

Our slogan is “Your Rebels in the Swamp.”

“Your” refers to our readers — the American people.

“Rebels” means we don’t toe the partisan line or adopt narratives just because they’re popular or convenient.

And “the Swamp” signals that we are in the heart of Washington, reporting the truth just blocks from the White House.

This rebellious spirit goes back to our founding. When political media was largely dominated by liberal cable outlets and progressive digital blogs, our founders had a vision for a new kind of conservative publication — one that would challenge the prevailing media narratives, break stories the establishment press ignored, and have a little fun while doing it.

That didn’t just apply to Democrats. One of the Caller’s first big scoops exposed the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) nearly $2,000 expenditure at a bondage-themed Hollywood nightclub.

Our commitment to the truth doesn’t change depending on who occupies the seats of power in the nation’s capital. Neither does our willingness to make powerful people uncomfortable.

And frankly, anyone who thought otherwise wasn’t paying attention.

So the online chatter that the Daily Caller is going through some sort of radical transformation has got it wrong. We’re not pivoting. We’re recommitting.

I haven’t seen our newsroom this excited about its mission in years. Our reporters know exactly what we’re trying to accomplish, and they’re fearless in pursuing the stories that matter.

That’s what a newsroom with a clear sense of purpose looks like.

I don’t expect everyone to agree with every story we publish.

In fact, over the past few months, we’ve increasingly been accused of being foreign-funded puppets, haters, or controlled opposition by folks who mistakenly viewed us as a member of their “team.”

So let me be clear now about whose team we are on:

Which brings me back to yesterday’s election results.

There will be no shortage of people assigning blame, questioning what went wrong, and declaring themselves or their faction the future of the party.

We can’t let those debates obscure the more important point:

What is the conservative movement actually trying to conserve, and what kind of country is it trying to build?

Is keeping the left out of power enough, or do we have a positive vision for America that leaves our children and grandchildren something worthwhile to inherit?

The Daily Caller isn’t interested in anointing Trump’s successor or pretending we have all the answers.

But we are going to make sure Washington can’t ignore the voices of ordinary Americans.

It would be a dereliction of duty to let the next chapter of conservatism be written exclusively by politicians, wealthy donors, consultants, and the loudest voices on social media.

The people who have to live with the consequences deserve a say, too.

WASHINGTON — A defiant Secretary of War Pete Hegseth fired back at plans to impeach him, declaring that he won’t back down.

The House is expected to vote on an impeachment resolution Hegseth that outgoing libertarian-leaning Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced in September when it gavels back into session next week.

Follow for live updates on the 2026 Midterm Elections

“Just like the president. We don’t back down. And that especially applies now,” Hegseth declared in a nearly six-minute video message filmed outside the Department of War.

At the War Department: We Stand.We Fight. We Defend the Republic. pic.twitter.com/Kkr0DazmCE

“This is not about me, but of course, the other side, in case you’ve noticed, they’re obsessed,” Hegseth went on. “A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice.”

Hegseth had campaigned against Massie in his primary — a highly unusual move for a Pentagon honcho. Massie justified his impeachment push against Hegseth by citing Hegseth’s role in the war in Iran.

Many Democrats have signaled plans to potentially impeach Hegseth when they roar back to power next year with one of the largest House majorities since at least 2008.

Rumors have swirled that Hegseth could step down and get an appointment by Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn to fill her soon-to-be vacant old Senate seat. Hegseth’s close allies have shot those rumors down.

The secretary of war also used his video message to push for lawmakers to pass additional funding for the Department of War.

This was supposed to be a wasted season for Steph Curry.

The Warriors were injury-riddled and coming off a lackluster summer in which they made no major moves.

It meant the greatest shooter of all time was destined to tread water as he turned 39 years old.

Yaxel Lendeborg changed everything.

He has resuscitated Curry’s career. He has breathed new life into a flailing dynasty. He has given the Warriors their future franchise star.

Lendeborg was a question mark when the Warriors selected him as the No. 11 pick in the 2026 draft.

Can a jack-of-all-trades turn into a star? Can a 24-year-old surpass expectations or has he already peaked? Can a rookie really be NBA ready?

Lendeborg has emphatically answered those questions.

He’s averaging 21.5 points (50% shooting from the field, 40% from 3), seven rebounds and 3.9 assists for the Warriors, who have won five games in a row.

The Warriors are good. Curry has a wingman. This is thrilling for anyone who loves basketball.

No one seems to be savoring this more than Curry, whose joy has been on full display amid the Warriors’ unexpected rise.

During his 44-point deluge against the Timberwolves on Oct. 28, Curry flashed a lunge pose after sinking a shot from beyond the arc.

After his jab sent Luka Doncic onto his butt and he swished a 3-pointer against the Lakers on Oct. 30, he did the Edvard Munch celebration, putting his hands on his cheeks and opening his mouth in shock.

And after scoring 34 points against the Suns on Monday, he didn’t hesitate when asked what has changed for the Warriors this season.

“I mean, Yax,” Curry said, flashing a smile.

Curry and Lendeborg are the NBA’s second-highest scoring duo (51.5 points per game), behind Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves (61.8). Lendeborg’s success has been a life raft for the Warriors, who are without Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody for the first few months of the season and without Kristaps Porzingis indefinitely.

In many ways, Lendeborg has unlocked Curry. He has made his brilliance count. He has lit a new fire under him.

Curry, who missed 27 straight games because of runner’s knee last season, is averaging 30 points (46.8% shooting from the field, 42.9% from beyond the arc), 4.2 rebounds and 4.5 assists per game.

He just surpassed Michael Jordan (44) for the most 40-point games in NBA history since turning 30, notching his 45th such performance last week.

Curry is playing as though he were a decade younger. And that’s because a guy 14 years younger than him is making all of this meaningful.

It’s funny because this really couldn’t have worked out better for both parties.

Curry, a two-time MVP and four-time champion, is doing what he loves most: winning.

And the outspoken Lendeborg has found a team that needs him to contribute immediately and encourages his bravado, two things that could’ve been problematic with other franchises.

Patience isn’t Lendeborg’s strong suit.

And neither is being politically correct.

The rookie recently raised eyebrows when he stunningly said he lost all respect for Dončić following their trash talk in the season opener. The Warriors didn’t wince.

Instead, Curry, Draymond Green and coach Steve Kerr unapologetically had his back.

Lendeborg landed in the perfect situation. He has a mentor in Green, who’s famous for unabashedly speaking his mind. And he has a franchise behind him with a win-now mentality that needs him to shine.

Lendeborg has found his home. He can flourish here. He needs to flourish here.

He has found his life preserver.

It’s in the form of a rookie who has made it so that instead of treading water he’s soaring.

And after scoring 34 points against the Suns on Monday, he didn’t hesitate when asked what has changed for the Warriors this season.

“I mean, Yax,” Curry said, flashing a smile.

Curry and Lendeborg are the NBA’s second-highest scoring duo (51.5 points per game), behind Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves (61.8). Lendeborg’s success has been a life raft for the Warriors, who are without Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody for the first few months of the season and without Kristaps Porzingis indefinitely.

In many ways, Lendeborg has unlocked Curry. He has made his brilliance count. He has lit a new fire under him.

Curry, who missed 27 straight games because of runner’s knee last season, is averaging 30 points (46.8% shooting from the field, 42.9% from beyond the arc), 4.2 rebounds and 4.5 assists per game.

He just surpassed Michael Jordan (44) for the most 40-point games in NBA history since turning 30, notching his 45th such performance last week.

Curry is playing as though he were a decade younger. And that’s because a guy 14 years younger than him is making all of this meaningful.

It’s funny because this really couldn’t have worked out better for both parties.

Curry, a two-time MVP and four-time champion, is doing what he loves most: winning.

And the outspoken Lendeborg has found a team that needs him to contribute immediately and encourages his bravado, two things that could’ve been problematic with other franchises.

Patience isn’t Lendeborg’s strong suit.

And neither is being politically correct.

The rookie recently raised eyebrows when he stunningly said he lost all respect for Dončić following their trash talk in the season opener. The Warriors didn’t wince.

Instead, Curry, Draymond Green and coach Steve Kerr unapologetically had his back.

Lendeborg landed in the perfect situation. He has a mentor in Green, who’s famous for unabashedly speaking his mind. And he has a franchise behind him with a win-now mentality that needs him to shine.

Lendeborg has found his home. He can flourish here. He needs to flourish here.

He has found his life preserver.

It’s in the form of a rookie who has made it so that instead of treading water he’s soaring.

Thanksgiving is right around the corner, and it might be time to consider giving your gut a little reboot before the real feasting begins. Some shoppers seem to have stumbled upon a solution — but not without a few side effects.

The product in question is Seed’s 14-Day Reset, which retails for $25 on Amazon and features 24 clinically and scientifically studied probiotic strains in a plant-based prebiotic outer capsule. According to the brand, the capsules are designed to support healthy gut function by reinforcing the gut barrier.

However, the supplement comes with a warning. Some users may experience “temporary gastrointestinal changes” as their body adjusts to the formula. Generally, the effects ease over time.

“After years of gut instability and near-liquid passing, I decided to give this a try,” one shopper shared. “Yes, it caused intense pressure and cramping in the left lower abdomen. It does note this on the packaging as well. But it changed my life!”

They went on to explain that the cramping eventually stopped, and they’ve now been “solid and regular” for about three months.

“I can go out to eat without stopping mid-meal to use the restroom. This might not be for the faint of heart but it absolutely worked,” they concluded.

Beyond regularity, other reviewers have noted that it has helped reduce bloating, while some even claim to have lost a few pounds since using it.

“Could be a coincidence but after a few days of taking this I lost 1-2 lbs and I’ve been tracking my weight all the time, so its surprising it hasn’t gone back up (water weight). My digestion seems better and overall I think my gut bacteria is getting better,” another user shared.

The brand suggests starting with two capsules daily for two weeks. If symptoms become severe, you can reduce the dosage to one capsule per day.

DS-01 Gut Reset is third-party tested for quality and safety. As with any supplement, be sure to consult a physiciain prioir to use — especially if you have any preexisting health conditions.

Ready to upgrade your wellness regimen? Vital Proteins collagen peptides are formulated to aid in supporting hair, skin, and nail health with collagen peptides made from grass-fed, pasture-raised bovine hides.

If you’re ready to crank up your NAD+ levels, the TRU NIAGEN PRO NAD+ is a great place to start. This formula is shown to increase NAD+ levels in three weeks and has decades of research behind it.

Formulated with 60 billion CFU and 10 diverse probiotic strains, Physician’s Choice Probiotics are designed to restore healthy gut flora, support digestion, and strengthen immune function.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Richard Barrera, the San Diego school board president backed by California’s powerful teachers union, has won the race for state superintendent of public instruction.

“Last night, voters made their choice,” Chino Valley school board president Sonja Shaw said Thursday as she conceded. “I would be lying if I said my heart wasn’t heavy. As a mother and a protector of children, I feel deeply saddened for the kids. They are the ones who deserve so much better,” she added.

Barrera led with 4,014,765 votes, about 57.6%, to Shaw’s 2,959,230, about 42.4%, a margin of more than 1 million votes, according to results updated Thursday morning. All precincts had reported their ballots.

“More than $10 million was poured into this race against us and we were up against a political machine that has been in place for decades. We didn’t have that kind of money or machinery,” Shaw said. “What we had were people. Mamas, dads, papas, Grammy bears, teachers, parents and everyday Californians who linked arms because they believe our children are worth fighting for.”

Barrera, 59, who has yet to make a public statement, steps into a now largely moot role that looks very different from the one outgoing Superintendent Tony Thurmond held.

Under a law Gov. Gavin Newsom signed this summer, the next governor will appoint an education commissioner to run the California Department of Education beginning in 2027 — removing the department oversight that has long defined the elected post.

The superintendent will instead become a voting member of the State Board of Education and join the California Community Colleges Board of Governors, while remaining a UC regent and CSU trustee.

The new superintendent and the commissioner are expected to spend the first six months of 2027 negotiating a job description to bring back to the Legislature.

Governor-elect Xavier Becerra will appoint the state’s first commissioner of education.

Neither candidate supported the overhaul.

Shaw called it an unconstitutional “power grab” and said she plans to sue to stop future governors from appointing a commissioner, though legal experts have said such a suit is unlikely to succeed.

Barrera was more accepting of the change and has pitched using the office to draft an education budget with local educators and parents before the governor releases his spending plan each January.

Shaw, 44, thanked her husband and two daughters but noted her work isn’t finished.

“I don’t know exactly what God has next, but I know He isn’t finished,” she said. “California’s kids still deserve an education that prepares them for life. Parents still deserve to be heard. Teachers deserve support. And our children deserve adults willing to stand up for them.”

“The election may be over, but the work and the mission don’t end here,” she added.

Shaw and Barrera advanced from a 10-candidate June primary that included several legislative veterans, among them Assemblyman Al Muratsuchi and former Assembly Speaker Anthony Rendon. Rendon later conceded and endorsed Barrera.

Shaw finished first with 22.6% of the vote, or roughly 1.74 million ballots. Barrera took 20.3%, about 1.56 million.

Shaw, who was elected to the Chino Valley Unified board in 2022 and was a stay-at-home mother before the pandemic, made headlines in 2023 when she presided over a board meeting at which Thurmond was escorted out during a heated debate over a policy requiring schools to notify parents if their child identifies as transgender.

California has since barred districts from enforcing such policies, a law Shaw wants to undo.

She also opposes allowing transgender girls to compete in girls’ sports and backs reinstating the SAT requirement for UC admissions.

She was endorsed by the California Republican Party, Moms for Liberty California and the California Rifle and Pistol Association.

Barrera, a longtime labor organizer, has served on the San Diego Unified board for 18 years and works as a senior adviser for special projects at the state Department of Education.

He supports Prop. 3, which would make permanent the high-earner income tax that funds schools, and has called for more counselors, nurses and smaller class sizes. He opposes bringing back the SAT requirement and supports the state’s LGBTQ+ student protections.

Barrera won the backing of the California Democratic Party and, unusually, both the California Teachers Association and its longtime rival, the California Charter Schools Association.

The CTA spent $8.4 million supporting Barrera and opposing Shaw, according to campaign finance records.

During an October debate hosted by EdSource, Barrera repeatedly tied Shaw to President Donald Trump, while Shaw accused him of “Trump derangement syndrome.”

Barrera has said Shaw used her platform to divide people and bully vulnerable students; Shaw has argued Barrera treats student outcomes as a talking point.

The Post has reached out to Barrera for comment.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

A beloved San Francisco staple that has spent nearly three decades feeding downtown office workers has been forced out of its long-running location after its corporate landlord pulled the rug out from the under the owners.

Oasis Grill, a family-owned Mediterranean eatery that has dished out gyros, shawarma wraps and kebabs since 1999, served its final meal at its 1st Street location last week, after their lease was handed to another restaurant, according to the San Francisco Standard.

“We were blindsided,” co-owner Muna Azzghayer told the outlet.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

While Oasis Grill survived the economic ups and downs of the city’s business district, it couldn’t survive its landlord.

Azzghayer and her husband, Mohammad Zughaiyir, told the Standard they were caught off guard when commercial real estate giant Kilroy Reality declined to renew their lease, which expired at the end of October. Instead, the landlord informed the couple that another restaurant would be taking over their longtime home.

The trouble began brewing earlier this year when building management started parading prospective tenants through the bustling storefront, according to Azzghayer.

When she pressed for answers about whether their lease was in jeopardy, management was reportedly silent.

Azzghayer believes the business fell victim to a ruthless bidding war, suspecting that the incoming tenant simply offered dollar figures the mom and mom eatery couldn’t match.

“They’re looking for more rent than what we’re paying, and they brought somebody else in and told us, basically, bye,” Azzghayer told the Standard. “We were committed to San Francisco, we believed in San Francisco, and I guess we paid the price for it.”

The eviction carries an especially brutal financial sting.

Back in 2015, the owners sank roughly $2 million and an entire year transforming the counter-service space from the ground up, including installing brand new commercial gas lines.

Shortly after completing the extensive overhaul, the business was pummeled by the COVID-19 pandemic, weathering years of cratered foot traffic and remote work policies that left the Financial District resembling a ghost town.

While the 1st Street location is gone, Oasis Grill still serves customers at three remaining San Francisco outposts on Drumm Street, 4th Street and Market Street.

news.title: Nithya Raman pays tribute to Karen Bass and thanks LA voters after winning race for mayor
news.originalSummary:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

DSA-backed Nithya Raman, the city councilmember who just unseated Mayor Karen Bass, paid tribute to her rival Thursday in her first public message as mayor-elect.

Raman posted a video on social media shortly after her victory was projected.

“I am honored to be your next mayor,” Raman said.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California

DSA-backed Nithya Raman, the city councilmember who just unseated Mayor Karen Bass, paid tribute to her rival Thursday in her first public message as mayor-elect.

Raman posted a video on social media shortly after her victory was projected.

“I am honored to be your next mayor,” Raman said.

The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

The mayor-elect then turned to the incumbent, tracing her career from the emergency room to City Hall.

“I also wanted to pay tribute to Mayor Karen Bass, someone who has given decades of her life to making this city what it is today,” Raman said.

She cited Bass’s time as an emergency-room nurse, her founding of Community Coalition, her leadership in Sacramento and Washington, and her election as the city’s first woman mayor.

“I know so many people, not just across this city but across this country, are grateful for her dedication to the promise of Los Angeles,” she said.

She saved her most direct appeal for voters who backed Bass, or sat the election out.

“I am going to City Hall to work every single day to earn your trust and to earn your trust in this city again,” Raman said.

She said that the work for her “starts now” to get housing people can afford, parks for children, a transit system that can “get people where they need to go,” and a city government “that is actually capable of delivering on its promises.”

“I love this city and I love its people, and I cannot wait to get started on building a better future together with all of you,” she said. “Thank you so much, Los Angeles.”

Earlier today, Bass conceded defeat and called Raman to congratulate her on her victory. She also pledged a smooth transition, saying Los Angeles voters had spoken despite the disappointing outcome.

“I love Los Angeles. I believe in Los Angeles. And I will continue to ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us. Thank you,” Bass said in her final message.

news.originalContent:

Two years after playing a major role in helping President Trump secure his 2024 win, Latino men have dramatically swung the other way.

Democrats swept the House and Senate in a Midterm massacre for the GOP Tuesday — and Latino men played a significant role in the historic sweep.

Follow for live updates on the 2026 Midterm Elections

NBC’s exit poll on Tuesday showed Latino men nationwide favored Democrats by 56%, compared to 41% for Republicans.

In 2024, NBC’s exit poll showed Latino men swinging right, favoring Republicans by 54% and Democrats by 44%.

Political commentator Samantha Karlin told The Post that Trump appealed to Latino men in 2024 with promises of “prosperity, strength, and security” — but said many are finding that those promises “haven’t translated into a better quality of life.”

She added that Trump’s immigration crackdown may have also played a role in the dramatic swing.

“There’s a profound difference between supporting border security and watching people who look like you, your family, and your neighbors being targeted by aggressive immigration enforcement,’ she said.

Karlin added that living with the fear that you or someone you love could be detained, regardless of legal status, creates “tremendous insecurity.”

“According to UnidosUS, 83% of Latino voters are struggling financially. The American Dream increasingly feels out of reach,” she continued.

“I think many Latino men are realizing that Trump’s strongman image doesn’t translate into economic security or protection for their communities.”

On Tuesday night, Republicans lost Senate races in traditionally red states Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas, with Democrats also securing the House.

In Texas, James Talarico made history by becoming the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from Texas since 1988, beating state Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Associated Press exit poll showed that 62% of voters blamed Trump’s policies for higher prices, with 71% saying Congress must do more to check the president.

“The Democrats did a good job,” Trump told Fox News. “They fought hard.”

He acknowledged the Iran war is partly to blame for the Republican losses.

“People agree with what I’m doing on Iran, but they really probably weren’t willing to do the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline. I understand that. I don’t agree with it,” he said.

news.originalSummary:
